headline: A rocket caught in mid-air, a doomsday that never came, and a capybara café
teaser: Can a rocket be reused like an airplane? Why did scientists once predict infinite people by 2026? And is petting a wild animal over coffee worth the risk?

articles.title: Caught in Mid-Air: SpaceX Catches a Returning Starship for the First Time
articles.dek: A giant rocket stage came home from orbit and was grabbed by its launch tower. Is this the start of cheap, routine spaceflight, or just a spectacular demonstration?
paras: On Saturday afternoon, November 14, a stainless-steel spacecraft roughly 50 meters tall dropped out of the sky over southern Texas, fired its engines and slowed almost to a stop beside its launch tower. Two enormous mechanical arms, nicknamed "chopsticks," closed around it and held it in place. It was the first time SpaceX had caught the upper stage of its Starship rocket after a trip to orbit, and a company commentator called the moment "the holy grail of spaceflight." The ship had lifted off about 22.5 hours earlier, circled the Earth repeatedly, and survived a fiery return through the atmosphere before the catch.

To understand why engineers were so excited, it helps to know how rockets have traditionally worked. For most of the space age, rockets were used only once: after launch, their stages fell into the ocean or burned up in the atmosphere, so every mission required building a new vehicle. Since the 2010s, SpaceX has reduced costs by landing and reusing the first stage of its smaller Falcon 9 rocket, but the upper stage, which travels much faster, has still been thrown away. Starship is designed to change that. If both of its stages can be recovered and flown again, launching a rocket could become more like operating an airliner than firing a firework, and the cost of reaching orbit could fall dramatically.

The test, Starship's fifteenth, did not go entirely to plan. The giant Super Heavy booster, powered by 33 Raptor engines, was supposed to fly back to the launch site a few minutes after liftoff and be caught by the tower as well, completing the first "double catch." Instead, the catch was called off, and the booster was sent to a splashdown zone in the Gulf of Mexico, where it was lost. The company has not fully explained why. The ship, meanwhile, reached low Earth orbit, released 26 of SpaceX's newest Starlink internet satellites, and orbited the planet about 14 times before heading home.

Supporters argue that the catch is a turning point. Catching a ship on the tower, rather than recovering it from the sea, means it can be inspected, refueled and launched again quickly, without a long journey back from an ocean landing site. SpaceX wants reusable Starships to launch thousands of satellites and, eventually, to carry people to the Moon and Mars; NASA has already selected Starship as a lunar lander for its Artemis program. Some analysts go further and argue that cheap, frequent launches could open entirely new industries, from space-based manufacturing to orbital data centers, much as cheap air travel transformed tourism and trade.

Not everyone is so optimistic. Critics point out that one successful catch is not the same as routine reuse: the ship must be refurbished and flown again, many times, before engineers can claim that the system works reliably. Several earlier Starship test flights ended in explosions, and in 2025 debris from two failed flights fell near islands in the Caribbean, forcing airlines to delay or divert flights. Environmental groups have also raised concerns about noise, disturbance to wildlife and the sheer number of launches SpaceX is planning from its site on the Texas coast, which sits next to protected wildlife habitat.

There is also a wider question about who controls access to space. As SpaceX's rockets become cheaper and more capable, government agencies are relying on a single private company for more of their missions. Supporters say this competition has saved taxpayers billions of dollars and pushed the whole industry forward. Others worry that it gives one company, and its founder, unusual influence over national space programs, communications networks and even military planning. If a small number of firms own the only affordable route to orbit, they ask, who will set the rules?

For now, the catch is best seen as an important milestone rather than a finished achievement. It shows that a spacecraft returning from orbit can be guided back with remarkable precision, but it also leaves big questions unanswered: how quickly the same ship can fly again, how much reuse will really reduce costs, and whether the benefits of a busier sky will outweigh its risks. The next few flights, and particularly the first time a caught ship is launched again, will reveal whether this was the start of a new era or simply a spectacular demonstration.

write.p: Professor: This week, SpaceX caught a returning Starship with its launch tower for the first time. Supporters say fully reusable rockets will make space travel cheap and open new industries. Critics point to failed test flights, environmental damage and the power of a single company. Should governments encourage private companies to lead space exploration, or should space remain mainly a government responsibility? Why? (Mia says: I think private companies should lead. Competition has already cut launch costs dramatically, and companies move faster than government agencies. Governments can still set safety rules without building every rocket themselves.) (Daniel says: I disagree. Space affects everyone, from satellites to the military. If one company controls the only cheap route to orbit, it could put profit before public interests. Governments should stay in charge of the most important missions.)
steps: Decide: private companies lead, or governments stay in charge.
Give one reason, such as cost and speed, or public control and safety.
Add an example, such as reusable rockets or satellite networks.
Respond to Mia or Daniel, then conclude in one sentence.

articles.title: Doomsday Postponed: The 1960 Prediction That Said Population Would Explode This Week
articles.dek: A famous scientific paper predicted that the number of humans would become infinite on Friday, November 13, 2026. Why was it wrong, and what does it teach us about trusting forecasts?
paras: Friday, November 13, 2026, was supposed to be the end of the world, at least according to a famous scientific paper. In 1960, the Austrian-American physicist Heinz von Foerster and two colleagues published an article in the respected journal Science with a dramatic title: "Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026." Their calculations suggested that, if the human population kept growing the way it had for the previous two thousand years, the number of people on Earth would effectively become infinite on that date. The day has now come and gone, the planet has roughly eight billion inhabitants rather than an infinite number, and the anniversary has become an opportunity to ask what the prediction got wrong and what it can still teach us.

The researchers' model was based on a striking observation. In ordinary exponential growth, a population doubles over a fixed period, for example every fifty years. Von Foerster's data, however, suggested that the human population was doubling faster and faster: it had taken many centuries to double in ancient times, but only decades in the modern era. The researchers argued that this was because a larger population could cooperate more effectively, invent better technology and produce more food, which in turn allowed the population to grow even faster. Mathematically, this kind of pattern, called hyperbolic growth, does not just rise steeply; it shoots toward infinity at a specific point in time.

Surprisingly, the formula worked well for several decades. When the paper appeared, there were about three billion people on Earth, and the model tracked actual growth reasonably closely through the 1960s and 1970s and into the 1980s. Historians note that its projections only began to clearly fail in the early 1990s. Even the date itself was partly a joke: it reportedly fell on von Foerster's birthday, and one mathematician has pointed out that the model's uncertainty was about five and a half years in either direction. Many experts believe the authors were making a provocative point about the dangers of uncontrolled growth rather than seriously forecasting the end of humanity.

The prediction failed because human beings are not particles obeying physical laws. Global population growth peaked at more than 2 percent a year in the early 1960s, just after the paper was published, and has slowed ever since. As countries became richer and more urban, child mortality fell, education spread, especially among women, and families increasingly chose to have fewer children. As the mathematical biologist Joel Cohen has put it, von Foerster "didn't allow for the possibility that people might choose to have fewer children." In other words, the model treated a social trend as if it were a law of nature.

Ironically, today's worries often point in the opposite direction. The United Nations projects that the world's population will peak at around 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s and then slowly decline. Many countries, including much of Europe and East Asia, now have fertility rates below the "replacement level" of about 2.1 children per woman, which raises concerns about aging societies, shrinking workforces and the cost of pensions and health care. Some commentators now warn of a population "bust" rather than a population bomb.

Yet experts caution against simply swapping one fear for another. Population is still growing quickly in some poorer countries; the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for example, is projected to double its population within about thirty years, which could put pressure on food and water supplies. Meanwhile, environmental scientists stress that the planet's problems depend not only on how many people there are but on how much each person consumes, and resource use is rising fastest in wealthier countries. Demographers also admit that fertility is extremely hard to forecast more than about a decade ahead.

Perhaps the most useful lesson of the doomsday paper is about the limits of prediction. A simple model can describe the past accurately and still fail badly in the future, because the people it describes can change their behavior, sometimes precisely because they have been warned. The same caution applies to today's forecasts about technology, economies and the environment. Good models are valuable tools for thinking, but they are not prophecies, and treating them as certain can be as misleading as ignoring them altogether.

articles.title: Cute but Risky? Animal Cafés Bring Wildlife Diseases Closer to Home
articles.dek: Petting a capybara over coffee is fun and makes a great photo. But when wild animals become entertainment, who pays the price: the visitors, the animals, or both?

sources.name: CIDRAP, on Gippet et al., Science (2026)

paras: In a café in Bangkok, customers sip iced coffee while a capybara, the world's largest rodent, wanders between the tables waiting to be fed. Nearby, visitors can stroke meerkats and bamboo rats. Animal cafés, petting zoos and exotic pet shows like these have become popular across Asia and beyond, and many of them attract crowds of young people eager to take photos for social media. But a new in-depth report by the environmental news site Mongabay argues that these close encounters may carry a hidden cost: they bring wild animals, and the germs they carry, into crowded public spaces.

Diseases that pass from animals to humans are known as zoonotic diseases, and they are far more common than many people realize. One recent review estimated that about 75 percent of new or re-emerging infectious diseases come from animals. Some, like rabies, have been known for centuries; others appear suddenly, as the Nipah virus did in Malaysia in the late 1990s, when it spread from bats to pigs and then to farmworkers. Scientists call the moment a pathogen first passes from an animal to a person a "spillover," and every close contact between people and wildlife is another chance for one to happen.

The evidence linking the wildlife trade to disease has been growing. A study published in the journal Science this year analyzed four decades of international trade records and found that wild mammal species sold in the trade were about 50 percent more likely to share pathogens with humans than species that were not traded. On average, each species gained one additional shared pathogen for every ten years it remained in trade. The lead author argued that buying and selling wild animals increases the risk of that first jump by bringing people into close and repeated contact with them, although another scientist noted that the study measured how long species were traded, not how many animals were sold.

Real outbreaks show how this can happen. In the United States, salmonella bacteria linked to pet geckos sickened 113 people in 36 states. In Belgium, fifteen customs officers caught psittacosis, a bacterial infection that can cause pneumonia, after handling infected parakeets. In 2025, authorities in Singapore seized 2,500 red-eared slider turtles carrying salmonella that were being smuggled to India; all of them had to be put down. None of these cases involved a dangerous new pandemic, but together they show that exotic animals often carry germs that can harm the people who handle them.

Experts say the main problem is not that every animal café is dangerous but that many operate with little oversight. Legally imported animals usually pass through quarantine and disease testing, whereas animals obtained through illegal trafficking often skip these checks entirely. One conservation researcher told Mongabay that well-run facilities with veterinary supervision may pose a relatively low immediate risk, but that new cafés and petting zoos "are appearing everywhere, and many are unregulated." In India, a recent report found that the country lacks a system to monitor imported animals for disease after they arrive.

Supporters of animal encounters see the issue differently. Operators often argue that children need to see and touch animals in order to develop compassion for them, and that a café or an educational show may be the only way many city children will ever meet a reptile or a rodent up close. Others point out that millions of people keep exotic pets without problems, and that basic hygiene, such as washing hands after contact, greatly reduces the risk. Banning these businesses outright, they warn, could simply push the trade underground, where it would be even harder to monitor.

Critics respond that the debate is not only about human health. Wild animals kept in noisy cafés may suffer stress, and using them as props for entertainment or teaching sends a questionable message about how wildlife should be treated. One animal-welfare campaigner argued that if animals are being used simply as a tool to teach a lesson, it may be time to rethink how that lesson is taught. For now, many experts favor a middle path: stronger licensing and veterinary checks, tighter controls on imports, and better public awareness, so that a cute photo does not come at the cost of an animal's well-being or a visitor's health.
